beliefs.title: Stay close to the build
beliefs.text: AI leadership is not status reports from 30,000 feet. You cannot govern what you do not understand at the level of the actual system.

beliefs.title: Data access is an org responsibility
beliefs.text: Every worker should reach trusted information with the right controls—SQL-savvy or not. Platforms exist to remove that friction.

beliefs.title: Transformation is architecture plus behavior
beliefs.text: Shipping technology is half the work. Changing how people decide, review, and operate is where value sticks.

beliefs.title: Judgment does not commoditize
beliefs.text: AI compresses the gap from idea to prototype. What remains scarce is knowing which prototype to scale and which tradeoff the business can live with.

beliefs.title: Operating rhythm is a product
beliefs.text: Reviews, decision rights, and experiment loops compound faster than any single feature. Design the cadence and ship it.

biography.title: Ishita Majumdar
biography.lede: Builder-executive. Three lengths of the same story—for introductions, press, and the full arc.
biography.summary:
I’m a rare executive who stepped away from traditional organizational leadership to build with AI from first principles, and my innate curiosity and exploration is what continues to shape how I lead today. 

Early in my career, I focused on architecting context-aware systems and later moved into modernizing data platforms to keep them agile, cutting-edge, and open source based. The work became deeply personal when I co-founded a startup centered on human-powered AI—building a support and care platform for families navigating special needs. Today, I lead global data and AI strategies, creating trusted, intelligent systems and inspiring a culture of data literacy and ethical AI adoption across enterprise teams. Yet I remain an active builder at heart, using modern AI tools every day for design, rapid prototyping, and QA, bringing that same authentic founder’s mindset to every level of leadership.

career.title: Chief Data and AI Officer — Relanto
career.text: Leading global data and AI strategy, building trusted, intelligent systems that transform how the enterprise makes decisions, automates workflows, and delivers customer value, while championing data literacy and ethical AI adoption.

career.title: Co-Founder / CPTO — Stealth Startup
career.text:
We started this company as three co-founders, inspired by our common experiences as care givers to children/young adults who have neuro-developmental conditions. With the advent of generative AI, we decided to build a prototype using LLM and see if we can build an agent focused on answering questions from families who are struggling to get advice on.... 

What to do when your child has a meltdown and we know she is on the spectrum?

Can I see a private behavioral therapist and not have to wait for 2 months, if I am willing to spend money from my pocket?

Can the government help? How?

Information was fragmented and un trusted. What if we can build a healthcare platform that is an integrated source of information, community, access to medical help and most importantly getting advice from folks who are trusted and experienced?

Product wise, it was great! GTM was it was not too great. It seemed after 2 years, that it should be a non profit

career.title: Vice President, Data Analytics Platforms — eBay
career.meta: Jan 2020 – Mar 2024 · San Francisco Bay Area
career.text:
By this time, I have spent many years in the data space. Enabling big data stack, using open source technology, for customer use cases in the telecom space. Defining and managing data products from Site DB, Data Analytics platforms, Data tools, Data preparation for ML algorithms. Realizing the massive importance of data from ingest to insights for better buyer and seller experience. Acknowledging how hard it is to maintain clean, compliant and trusted data for all consumers. The SQL savvy users: the Developers, the Analysts. The non SQL savvy users like the product managers, sales, business development managers. Increasingly, I believed that Data in any form should be accessible by any enterprise worker - with the right controls and access of course. It should be the Data org's responsibility to make this possible.  Hence it was a natural career transition for me to lead the data organization including data engineers, data scientists and data product managers on this journey to make data and data derivatives - accessible by everyone independently. For this, I added my three steel threads on how to achieve this.

  1. Build an A+ team. I pursued external and internal candidates with equal gusto so that can complement each other in their passion for getting the best out of data. My golden rule: hire no-ego, smart people who can work as a team.
  2. Be accountable for making data work for others. Data consumers should trust the data for any use case
  3. Be transparent with Data measures. That means sit with our customers to jointly determine KPIs and then keep on measuring them and publish the dashboards for all to see. No hiding!

career.title: Global Head of Technology Products — eBay
career.text:
I joined eBay to manage the Data Products from infrastructure to analytics to data tools. My technical expertise was in the data analytics space and very soon extended I learned to understand how experiment platforms work for decision making and how personalization platforms collect behavior signals and deliver "next best action".


How do we build the right platform to collect the true signals and separate from noise? 

How can we conduct faster experiments and better hypothesis testing?

How do we deliver in biweekly sprints and have better output and adoption?

How do we set up the right process for customer escalations?


My portfolio extended over time to include the entire tech stack from metal to ML. Datacenter & Network, Cloud and Security, AI/ML Platform, Developer tools. As I built the team, I realized this will be a unique combination of technical product managers and technical program managers alike. The Product managers were responsible for product vision, strategy, roadmap, customer engagement and stakeholder management. These folks transitioned from engineering careers to become dedicated product managers so they understood the technology, had the domain knowledge to challenge

bios.short: Ishita Majumdar is a builder-executive with 25+ years across engineering, product, data platforms, and enterprise AI transformation. She builds the systems, platforms, and organizations that turn Data + AI into measurable business outcomes—and stays close enough to the technical work to lead with judgment, not slideware.
bios.medium: Ishita Majumdar is a technology executive who progressed from engineering complex systems to platform building, product leadership, data executive roles, and AI transformation leadership. Over more than twenty-five years—including senior roles at eBay, technology strategy at Huawei, and three U.S. patents—she has scaled trusted data platforms, product organizations, and global teams. She co-founded a human-centered AI startup for families navigating special needs, then returned to enterprise leadership as Chief Data and AI Officer at Relanto. Her throughline is consistent: stay close to the build, make trusted data usable for every worker, and treat transformation as architecture plus behavior so AI delivers durable business outcomes rather than pilots that never leave the lab. Named a Top 10 Data Innovator and CDO Magazine Global Data Power Woman, she mentors first-time builders while leading enterprise intelligence strategies that connect platforms, people, and measurable results.

schools.title: The University of Chicago, Booth School of Business
schools.blurb: A Mathematician's detour into finance and strategy learning to speak the language of the business side of technology.
schools.learned: Booth taught me to reason from first principles about markets and capital, not just systems. The frameworks I still use to connect a technical roadmap to revenue and efficiency outcomes.

schools.title: Northern Illinois University
schools.blurb: Deepened the theoretical foundation of Mathematics and taught me to explore unknowns.
schools.learned: Pure mathematics builds a tolerance for sitting with a hard, unsolved problem, a habit that's paid off in every ambiguous, first-of-its-kind system I've since had to architect.

schools.title: Clemson University
schools.blurb: Where optimization theory turned into a practical toolkit for making systems and decisions more efficient.
schools.learned: Operations research is the art of finding the best decision under real constraints, the same lens I bring to platform architecture and to leading teams under tight timelines and budgets.

schools.title: Jadavpur University
schools.blurb: Where it all started, the foundation that made everything after it possible.
schools.learned: Rigor first. A proof either holds or it doesn't, that early standard for evidence and precision still shapes how I evaluate ideas today.

aiJourney.story:
I am a creator at heart. I like rolling up my sleeves, testing new tools, and building ideas into reality. The first few tries were laborious but with the help of some excellent workshops and You Tube free classes, I learned how to explore, experiment and get better.

I'm a rare executive who stepped away from organizational leadership to build with AI from first principles. No matter what my role is, I still stay in the build and I stay grounded in what's real. And this gives me the inspiration to mentor and inspire other first time builders.

books.title: Books that stay with me
books.lede: Reading is a constant for me, usually a book every month across fiction and non-fiction. Here are a few favorites that have stayed with me over time and that I continually return to for inspiration.

items.title: Think Again
items.author: Adam Grant
items.summary: This book reinforced my belief in trying something new and completely radical and see what happens. I challenged my old way of thinking, and experimented with my Data team in one of our offsites, where we went around the table inviting opinions from all on how to modernize the data stack thinking again, this time differently. I often go back to the examples in this book to get courage, inspiration and most importantly validation for rethinking and redoing and evolving as a technologist and a human being. "Rethink" gave me the courage to be a founder, to take risks and continue my zig-zag career and be comfortable in NOT conforming to the path that is always taken.

items.title: My Life in Full
items.author: Indra Nooyi
items.summary: I have always been a big fan on Indra Nooyi and always wanted to meet her in person for a chat. Instead, I met her through her book and it absolutely filled me with joy and admiration as I turned the pages. Her childhood, her parents, grandparents, all seemed to remind me of my life too (although we are from two different parts on India). Even in her meteoric rise in her professional career, she somehow did not lose her sense of humor and remained grounded as a person playing many many roles all at once. Reading this book was similar to being wrapped up in a cozy blanket which I have for 20 years now sipping a cup of tea and nodding my head at the beautiful narrative which painted familiar pictures in my head.

items.title: The Second Mountain
items.author: David Brooks
items.summary: I came across "Second Mountain" at a time when I was embarking on a founder's journey without any kind of start-up experience whatsoever. All I knew was, I need to build something for parents with neurodiverse dependents, so that they get peace of mind. And I could do it leveraging gen AI and the myriad tools that it provided. To me, this was my second mountain, something purposeful and meaningful that was bigger than me. Reading the book was an eye opener in to myself in many ways. What drives me? What gives me purpose? What makes me happy? This is also a book which I have gifted to at least 10 people as I thought it will motivate them as well

items.title: The Running Ground
items.author: Nicholas Thompson
items.summary: I am not a runner, married to one, yes but running is not something I like. Yet this book captured me from the very beginning. Because it fundamentally talks about human endurance and the mindset required to tackle long, challenging paths. It was a metaphor for life's larger marathons. That could be navigating complex career pivots, building something meaningful from scratch, or supporting loved ones when they go through difficult times (I have experienced all three). It keeps on making the point, not to judge yourself on how well you did in the short sprints but try and maintain your pace every day so that there is happiness in the pursuit of the challenge, not necessarily beating the clock.

items.title: GRIT
items.author: Angela Duckworth
items.summary: I honestly did not understand the meaning of GRIT till I read the book. I always thought, one is born talented. You are exceptional at Math, you are a born tennis player, you are ahead of your age group in piano. You are a natural genius. This book taught me, even with teh natural credentials, what sustains you throughout life is your perseverance and your efforts. You have to relentless. You have to be passionate. You have to be patient. I also used a lot of GRIT examples as a parent and introduced "deliberate practice" in the vocabulary of the family.

items.title: Shoe Dog
items.author: Phil Knight
items.summary:
Listening to Phil Knight's memoir on Audiobooks was like watching "Oceans Eleven". It was non stop adrenaline of executing improbable bets, surviving near collapse and working on your instincts to create a market which you are betting on to begin with. Most importantly I learned how to turn a side hustle into a global brand. There is no bluebook for this type of conviction and madness. At no step, was their assurance and certainty except in Knight's mind.

I keep it as a reminder that momentum often arrives before certainty: ship, adjust, stay loyal to the craft, and accept that the path will look messier than the brand story that comes later.

items.title: The Audacity of Hope
items.author: Barack Obama
items.summary:
I read this in 2008 a year, when my entire team was let go in a matter of one 20 minute team meeting. We were considered the elite if the elites, we were building the business in new and disruptive ways, we had this sense of invulnerability. Suddenly, we didn't exist. So I desperately needed Hope. This book was like a field guide for holding competing truths at once. It is about hope as discipline the hard work of listening and experiencing something you don't agree with, without abandoning conviction.

I keep returning to how he frames responsibility, to community, to institutions, and to the unfinished American story. Even when the policy landscape has shifted, the underlying invitation remains useful for anyone leading through ambiguity: argue in good faith, stay curious about people who disagree with you, and refuse the cheap comfort of cynicism. I lean on this book when I have to build consensus to achieve something Or I have to resolve conflicts without showing bias.

items.title: Radical Candor
items.author: Kim Scott
items.summary:
As a manager. one of the hardest things I learned was to how to give honest feedback with a belief that this actually helps in the development of people a nd teams. Kim Scott's framework for caring personally while challenging directly is a practical antidote to both sugarcoated praise and blunt cruelty at work. I learned to treat feedback as a relationship skill, something you practice in real conversations, not a performance-review ritual.

I return to it when coaching or being coached: say the hard thing early, stay on the person's side, and notice when silence is actually the unkind option.

items.title: Sapiens a Brief History of Mankind
items.author: Yuval Noah
items.summary:
Harari's sweep from cognitive revolution to data-driven empires is less a history textbook than a provocation about the stories humans invent to cooperate at scale. Money, nations, corporations, and gods all appear as shared fictions with real consequences.

Reading it sharpened how I think about technology leadership: tools do not merely optimize; they rewrite the myths organizations live by. It is a useful companion when you are building systems that will outlast a quarter's roadmap and reshape how people trust information, institutions, and each other.

items.title: Hit Refresh
items.author: Satya Nadella
items.summary:
Nadella's account of Microsoft's cultural reset is a case study in leading through empathy, learning, and partnering rather than defending the old playbook. It connects personal story to enterprise transformation—growth mindset as an operating system for a company that had to reinvent how it competes.

Useful anytime an organization needs to refresh identity without discarding what still works: listen harder, ship cloud-first bets, and measure culture by how people treat curiosity and collaboration.

musings.title: Featured perspectives
musings.lede: Short theses on AI transformation, data platforms, and how organizations actually change.

items.title: Shift Left or Shift Right - who wins?
items.body:
Remember the traditional role a Product Manager used to play? They talked with the customers, understood their pain points, defined the problem statement, prioritized against business goals, wrote the requirements in the Production Requirements Document (PRD) and then handed it over to design and engineering. They explored the "what" and the "why" of the product while dev teams focused on "how". Once the product was ready to build, the same PMs would be defining and managing roadmaps, collaborating with customers, partners and all stakeholders connected with the product, managing campaigns and launches and then measuring adoption after the launch. 

Then Gen AI emerged and Product Managers are able to shift right. AI lets them prototype, test with users and iterate without waiting on engineering. Engineers are also shifting left. AI lets them write the specs, do the mock ups, build, test and whip without waiting for a PRD. Both sides are arguing that the other one is redundant. Engineers argue, Product Managers should just do discovery. The "PMs should just do discovery" argument assumes execution is where the scarce value now lives, so whoever builds, wins. That's definitely backwards. The PMs argue, engineers should just do builds. That is not inspiring either, because engineers are able to build teh best products if they genuinely understand the requirements from a customer's perspective. Both observations are true but the conclusion isn't. 

What's actually happening is that AI is compressing the gap between idea and product for everyone, not handing one role's territory to the other. A PM prototyping in an AI tool and an engineer generating a spec from a ticket are doing the same thing from opposite ends: skipping a handoff that used to require the other person.

While "execution"is getting commoditized every other week or so,  what doesn't commoditize is judgment: which prototype is worth scaling, which tradeoff to make when the model's answer works but is wrong for the business, which customer signal is real. That takes context, honed by human PMs across customers, market, cost, org politics.  AI doesn't have that today and doesn't accumulate the way a person embedded in the problem does.

Cutting PMs down to discovery-only strips them of the prototyping loop that sharpens that judgment. And an engineer who never talks to a customer builds fancy systems that solve the wrong problem.

So neither role wins as a category. The people who lose are whoever refuses to touch the other side; the PM who won't prototype, the engineer who won't talk to customers. The people who win are whoever operates across the whole idea-to-shipped loop and uses AI to erase the handoff, not defend it.
items.thesis: Remember the traditional role a Product Manager used to play?

items.title: Can we interview for judgment?
items.body:
Open any executive resume and you're reading a highlight reel: revenue grown, teams scaled, deals closed. Nobody puts "shut down the product I championed for two years" in a bullet point. Nobody leads an interview with the hire they pushed for who cost the company its best engineer. We've built an entire hiring apparatus — resumes, LinkedIn, reference calls, panel interviews — that rewards narrative curation over honest accounting. And then we act surprised when we hire executives who can't say "I was wrong" once they're in the seat.

This isn't a minor blind spot. It's a structural one. What gets rewarded in hiring gets reproduced in leadership.

The "halo effect" where one strong positive signal (a prestigious employer, a polished pitch, a confident answer) colors every other judgment an interviewer makes, is one of the best-documented distortions in hiring research. A candidate who tells a clean success story gets read as competent across the board, even in areas the interview never actually tested. A candidate who admits a costly failure, unprompted, risks being read as a liability, even when the honesty itself is the more useful data point. So candidates learn, correctly, to suppress the failure and inflate the win. We've trained our best people to lie by omission, and then we hand them budgets.

Success stories are noisy. They conflate skill, timing, and luck, and a good storyteller can make any outcome sound earned. Failure is harder to spin. How someone describes a failure, what they think caused it, what they missed, what they'd do differently, whether they blame the market or own the call, tells you more about their judgment than almost anything else in an interview. Melanie Stefan, the biologist who popularized the public "CV of Failures" in 2010, and Johannes Haushofer, the Princeton professor whose failure CV went viral in 2016, weren't doing a branding exercise. They were making a point: the successes on a normal CV are a survivorship sample of one, and they hide the actual decision-making process. Executive hiring has the same flaw, at higher stakes.

As has been said before, "Create a Safe Environment". A safe environment doesn't mean zero-consequence disclosure, where any failure is automatically forgiven because it was mentioned. That's not safety, it's grade inflation with extra steps, and sophisticated candidates will game it by manufacturing humble-brag failures ("I worked too hard and burned out my team"). Real safety means the failure is evaluated on the same rigor as the success: what happened, what was in the candidate's control, what changed afterward. Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety is instructive here. Safety isn't the absence of accountability, it's the presence of a norm where surfacing a problem doesn't end your standing in the room. That's a much higher bar than "be nice about it," and it's the bar hiring processes should be held to.

Practically, this means changing the interview, not just the vibe. Ask every executive candidate for a specific, costly failure and hold that answer to the same structured rubric used for their wins. Ask yourself as an interviewer, what does this reveal about judgment, ownership, and adaptation. Normalize a standing question, asked the same way every time, so disclosure isn't a gamble an individual candidate takes alone. Train interviewers to notice when they're penalizing honesty relative to a slicker candidate who simply didn't mention their own version of the same mistake. And separate the discomfort of the story from the judgment of the person. A bad outcome and bad judgment are not the same thing, and conflating them is exactly what teaches people to stop disclosing.

The alternative is what we already have: executives who arrive polished and untested in the one skill that actually predicts how they'll handle the next real crisis, because we never asked them to demonstrate it, and we punished them, subtly, when they tried.
items.thesis: Open any executive resume and you're reading a highlight reel: revenue grown, teams scaled, deals closed.

items.title: Data vs Data
items.body:
We have started using the word "data" as if it were one substance. It is not. Machine-generated data (MGD) and human-generated data (HGD) may share schemas, pipelines, and dashboards, but they do not share the same moral weight, evidentiary value, or ownership story. Treating them as interchangeable is becoming one of the quieter risks in modern AI systems.

Human-generated data carries biography. It is created by people acting with intent—or at least with presence: a click, a sentence, a medical note, a photo, a transaction. Even when it is messy, biased, or incomplete, HGD is tethered to lived experience. That tether creates accountability. Someone can usually answer: who produced this, under what consent, in what context, and with what expectation of privacy?

Machine-generated data is different. It may be synthetic text, simulated telemetry, model embeddings, auto-labeled corpora, or outputs that look indistinguishable from human work. MGD can be extraordinarily useful for testing, augmentation, and scale. It can also launder uncertainty. When a model invents a pattern and we store that pattern as "data," we risk promoting a hypothesis into a fact without the social process that used to accompany evidence.

Ownership gets complicated fast. If an employee writes a strategy memo, the company may own the document under ordinary work-product norms. If that memo is later summarized by a model, and the summary is stored as training residue or product memory, who owns the derivative? If a customer uploads confidential material and a system generates synthetic variants "inspired by" it, have we created a new asset—or a new liability? The industry's instinct is to answer with license text. Leaders should answer with operating principles.

A practical principle: separate provenance from utility. Utility asks whether the data helps a model perform. Provenance asks whether we can defend how it came to exist. For HGD, provenance usually means consent, purpose limitation, retention, and access control. For MGD, provenance means disclosing that it is synthetic, documenting the generator, recording the seed inputs when relevant, and refusing to present simulated records as observational truth.

Accountability follows the same split. With HGD, privacy and confidentiality responsibilities sit with the collectors and processors who touched the human source. With MGD, responsibility does not disappear just because no single person "authored" the row. Someone chose the generator, the prompts, the filters, and the decision to put synthetic content into a production path. That someone still owns the blast radius if the synthetic content leaks, misleads, or contaminates evaluation sets.

Differentiating synthetic from real data is no longer a research nicety; it is an operational control. Label it at creation. Carry the label through transforms. Make it visible in catalogs and lineage graphs. Ban silent mixing in any workflow where legal discovery, clinical safety, financial audit, or customer trust depends on knowing what actually happened.

The deeper leadership question is not whether MGD will grow—it will. The question is whether we build institutions that can still tell the difference between a mirror and a person. Data vs data is not a naming debate. It is a test of whether we still know what we are responsible for.
items.thesis: We have started using the word "data" as if it were one substance.

items.title: Watermarking introduced by Anthropic?
items.body:
Watermarking has re-entered the AI conversation with new urgency: if a model provider can quietly mark outputs, what does that mean for authenticity, trust, and control? Anthropic's work and public discussion around watermarking sit inside a larger industry push to make AI-generated content detectable. The idea is appealing on its face. Society wants signals. Educators, publishers, and enterprises want provenance. Platforms want a way to distinguish synthetic media from human work without relying only on brittle classifiers.

But watermarking is not neutral infrastructure. It is a power move encoded as a technical feature. Whoever can apply, verify, or refuse a watermark shapes the evidentiary story around a piece of content. That can be protective—helping people spot machine-written text or edited media. It can also be coercive if the mark travels with work the user reasonably considers their own.

Consider a common enterprise workflow. You upload an original strategy deck you wrote. You ask Claude to tighten the narrative, redesign a section, or generate alternative slides. The final artifact is a hybrid: your ideas, your confidential framing, and model-assisted edits. If a watermark appears on the exported result, whose signature is that, exactly? The model provider's? The assistant's? Yours with an asterisk?

This is where thoughtful people diverge. One view says providers have a legitimate interest in marking machine contribution so downstream systems can detect synthetic influence, especially as deepfakes and automated propaganda scale. Another view says the user supplied the core intellectual property and confidential context; a vendor should not brand, track, or claim semiotic ownership over a derivative the customer will present as internal work product. Both views can be partly right. Neither should be settled by marketing copy alone.

There are also practical repercussions. Watermarks invite workarounds: paraphrase loops, cross-model rewriting, screenshotting, re-typesetting, adversarial scrubbing. A watermark that is easy to remove becomes theater. A watermark that is hard to remove may overreach into user content and create fragility when legitimate editing is needed. Detection systems can false-positive on heavily edited human writing, and false-negative on lightly touched synthetic text. Organizations that treat watermark presence as legal or HR proof will eventually discover how thin that proof can be.

I am not offering legal advice. Contract terms, jurisdiction, and product settings matter, and rights around model outputs are still being tested in courts and legislatures. What I am arguing for is product and procurement clarity. Enterprises should ask vendors directly: When is a watermark applied? Does it attach to fully user-authored uploads that were only lightly edited? Can customers disable it for confidential workflows? What metadata leaves the tenant boundary? How are disputes handled when a mark implies machine authorship of something a human largely wrote?

The deeper issue is stewardship. AI providers are becoming infrastructure for knowledge work. Infrastructure that silently annotates customer artifacts changes the meaning of authorship. Watermarking may be necessary for a trustworthy internet. It should not become a quiet claim of custody over the documents people bring into the model. The healthy outcome is layered provenance—user ownership preserved, machine contribution disclosed, and detection treated as a signal rather than a verdict.
items.thesis: Watermarking has re-entered the AI conversation with new urgency: if a model provider can quietly mark outputs, what does that mean for authenticity, trust, and control?

items.title: The Consultancy Paradox
items.body:
Claude and tools like it can already draft the memo, outline the operating model, synthesize the interview notes, and produce a slide narrative that would have taken a junior team a weekend. On paper, that should hollow out professional services. Why pay for a deck when a model can give you twelve versions before lunch?

And yet the demand for good consultants has not evaporated. In some domains it is intensifying. That is the paradox: as generative AI compresses the production of artifacts, it raises the value of judgment about which artifacts matter.

Consultancy was never only document manufacture. The best engagements sell clarity under political constraint. A client does not primarily need more text. They need someone who can walk into a room of competing incentives, name the real problem without flinching, and sequence change so the organization can absorb it. Models are strong at pattern completion. They are weaker at reading the unspoken veto, the board dynamic, the union history, the founder's grief, or the regulatory landmine that never made it into the brief.

There is also liability theater versus liability reality. An internal team can accept a model's recommendation more easily when an outside partner has stress-tested it, put their reputation behind the tradeoffs, and stayed present through implementation bruises. Professional services, at their best, are a commitment technology: someone agrees to be accountable when the tidy framework meets the messy org chart.

AI does change the shape of the work. Commodity analysis, first-draft research, and templated benchmarking get cheaper. That should push firms—and independent advisors—up the stack toward diagnosis, facilitation, decision design, and capability building. The consultant who only sells polished slides is in trouble. The consultant who uses AI to spend more time on stakeholder truth-seeking, options framing, and execution coaching is not.

Clients will still seek help for three stubborn reasons. First, perspective from outside the building. Second, skilled human mediation when incentives collide. Third, borrowed courage: sometimes leaders know the answer and need a partner to help the institution hear it. None of those are fully automatable, because they are social acts.

So the paradox resolves into a filter. AI reduces the market for performative expertise and expands the market for earned judgment. If your value was formatting certainty, you are being disrupted. If your value was helping people decide and deliver under uncertainty, you just got a sharper instrument—and a higher bar.
items.thesis: Claude and tools like it can already draft the memo, outline the operating model, synthesize the interview notes, and produce a slide narrative that would have taken a junior team a weekend.

art.title: My Art Collage
art.lede: I create art purely for the joy, energy, and freedom it gives me. Without a fixed style, I love experimenting with different medium, from acrylics and oils to pastels and fine-line pens and moving fluidly across styles like portraits, abstract, and cubism. For me, creating art is a feeling of total liberation: a safe place for unfettered exploration without worrying about success, failure, or external judgment.

items.title: Abstract wall art
items.summary: This wall collage in our home is a collection of piecework brought together by my pieces and some amazing contributions from my daughter and a close artist friend. There wasn't a grand plan behind it, just an organic mix of colors, styles, and shared harmony. Over the years, it has become the backdrop to countless family photos and celebrations.

items.title: Abstract cubism experiment
items.summary: Acrylic on canvas. Created in a single sitting, this triptych was driven by a linear challenge: lean heavily into line work and let the form evolve naturally, whether the final output being bizzarre  kaleidoscopes patterns or cubic faces. It’s about embracing bold, clashing colors and layering down paint without fear or second-guessing.

items.title: Corked wine glass
items.summary: This mixed-media piece came out of a lockdown realization. My wine cork collection had accelerated quite a bit during COVID, so I decided to turn lemons into lemonade or in this case, a tongue-in-cheek Greek-style goblet The most fun part was using a dripper to lay down a mix of real wine and glue, giving the canvas a uniquely sticky, freshly-poured look.

items.title: Covid Diary
items.summary: During the hardest stretches of COVID, I started creating these quick daily art pieces as a cathartic outlet. Using markers, colored pencils, crayons, or whatever was at hand, I spent 10 to 15 minutes capturing the exact mood of the day be it anger, frustration, Mother’s Day, or Christmas. These were spontaneous bursts of unfiltered emotions. The art was messy, amateur and one try only.  If art could be translated to emotional text, it would be like reading my journal on some very hard days.

items.title: Hide and Seek
items.summary: Inspired by a museum piece, I intentionally exaggerated the oversized hats to fully camouflage the figures, deepening the sense of mystery, elegance, and allure.

items.title: Veiled Face
items.summary: This artwork is a personal take on traditional Madhubani art, known for its fine lines and geometric patterns. I added my own spin with a confetti-like overlay, creating the impression of a heavy veil draped over beauty and raw emotion.

items.title: Peacock Plumage
items.summary: Using leftover house paint on our concrete walkway, I decided to turn an ordinary side path into something that brings an instant smile. I layered white and red brush strokes with delicate, raindrop-style flourishes to capture the rich, intricate feel of a peacock’s feathers.

hiking.title: On the trail
hiking.lede: Adventures, summits, and the routes that stuck with me.

trips.name: Grand Canyon — Descent to Arizona River
trips.meta: South Rim, AZ · Bright Angel / South Kaibab to Colorado River · Strenuous
trips.story:
A full descent from the South Rim toward the canyon floor — the river everyone means is the Colorado, even when we casually say "Arizona River." Switchbacks, heat, and a scale that resets your sense of distance.

Starter note for a personal blurb later: the moment the green ribbon of water finally appears below the red walls.

trips.name: Grand Canyon Rim to Rim Hike
trips.meta: North Rim ↔ South Rim, AZ · ~21–24 mi · Strenuous / multi-day option
trips.story:
Crossing the canyon from rim to rim is less a single hike than a negotiation with elevation, water, and daylight. North Rim forests give way to desert inner canyon, then the long climb out the other side.

Placeholder for the day-by-day story — logistics, pace, and what the corridor looked like when the walls closed in.

trips.name: Machu Picchu Hike
trips.meta: Cusco Region, Peru · Inca Trail / classic approach · High altitude
trips.story:
The approach to Machu Picchu — stones, mist, and the sudden reveal of the citadel on the ridge. Altitude does half the talking; the Andes do the rest.

Starter description until the personal travel notes land: the first clear view of the terraces after the final climb.

trips.name: Half Dome Hike
trips.meta: Yosemite National Park, CA · ~14–16 mi · Strenuous (cables)
trips.story:
Cables, granite, and a summit that makes every prior training hike feel like rehearsal. The Mist Trail or John Muir approach, then the exposed final pitch that defines the day.

Worth every early alarm — personal highlights to fill in later.

trips.name: Mission Peak
trips.meta: Fremont, CA · ~6 mi round trip · Hard
trips.story:
The local proving ground. Steep, crowded on weekends, and still the climb that resets a week of meetings into something simpler: one foot, then the next.

The iconic summit pole and East Bay views — more personal notes to come.

trips.name: Yosemite Hikes
trips.meta: Yosemite National Park, CA · Valley & high country classics · Mixed difficulty
trips.story:
A catch-all for Yosemite days beyond Half Dome — valley floor walks, waterfall trails, and granite overlooks that make the park feel endless.

Starter card for the trip collage; individual route notes can be split out later if needed.

trips.name: Dipsea Trail
trips.story: Stairs, redwoods, and the sudden reveal of the Pacific. A reminder that the best routes refuse to stay at one elevation — literal or otherwise.

items.name: Skills Intelligence HR App

items.why: Explore how AI agents can reason over workforce skills supply and demand.
items.tech: Claude agent, web app, skills catalog
items.learned: Conversational analysts need clean domain models—not just a chat box.

items.name: Aurora Health Agent
items.summary: A specialized virtual health agent for Autism Spectrum Disorder — evidence-based information with a smooth experience and graceful handling of varied user input.
items.why: Give families navigating ASD a calmer, evidence-aware first stop for questions.
items.learned: Graceful handling of messy human input matters as much as model quality.

items.name: AI News Agent
items.summary: An intelligent agent that scrapes the latest AI developments and summarizes them across infrastructure (hardware, compute, MLOps) and frontier models.
items.why: Keep a weekly pulse on infrastructure and frontier-model news without drowning in feeds.
items.learned: Curation beats volume; the product is the filter.

items.name: Racing Car Summary
items.summary: An AI news agent with a twist — shipping a working agent that digests and summarizes what matters, race-day energy included.
items.why: Ship a playful news agent end-to-end to practice agent packaging and hosting.
items.learned: Shipping fast teaches more than another architecture diagram.

items.name: Wiki MCP
items.summary: A Model Context Protocol server that gives Claude real-time Wikipedia access — search, fetch, and research tools built to learn core MCP concepts.
items.why: Learn Model Context Protocol by giving Claude live Wikipedia tools.
items.learned: Tool design is product design for agents.

items.name: Lighthouse
items.summary: A full-stack app for discovering and tracking high-impact AI trends — Next.js frontend, FastAPI backend, MongoDB, and OpenAI.
items.why: Track high-impact AI trends with a full-stack research loop.
items.learned: Trend products fail without disciplined ingestion and ranking.

items.name: Audiobook
items.summary: Convert any text into professional AI-generated audio using OpenAI's text-to-speech API — React frontend with an Express backend.
items.why: Turn arbitrary text into listen-able audio for accessibility and speed.
items.learned: Simple APIs still need careful UX around latency and voice quality.

items.title: Data & AI leadership in the enterprise
items.blurb: Conversations on trusted data platforms, ethical AI adoption, and leading transformation without losing the builder’s edge.

impact.title: Selected impact
impact.lede: Case studies, not job descriptions—challenge, what was built, and the outcome.

items.title: Making enterprise data usable at scale
items.challenge: Data lived in silos; analysts and non-SQL users could not independently trust or access the signals they needed for buyer and seller decisions.
items.action: Built and led the Data Analytics Platforms org—engineers, scientists, and product managers—around three steel threads: A+ teams, accountable data quality, and transparent KPIs.
items.impact: Scaled trusted analytics platforms serving the marketplace; made data and derivatives accessible across technical and business consumers with clear ownership.

items.title: From data products to full-stack tech platforms
items.challenge: Fragmented ownership across experiment platforms, personalization, and infrastructure slowed delivery and diluted product accountability.
items.action: Grew Global Head of Technology Products from data products into a portfolio spanning datacenter to ML—pairing technical PMs with TPMs for vision, roadmap, and adoption.
items.impact: Unified product systems for experimentation and personalization; biweekly delivery rhythm with clearer escalation paths and stakeholder engagement.

items.title: Enterprise intelligence as an operating system
items.challenge: Enterprises need AI that transforms decisions and workflows—not isolated pilots that never leave the lab.
items.action: As Chief Data and AI Officer, leading global data and AI strategy: trusted systems, ethical adoption, and literacy so teams can automate and decide with confidence.
items.impact: Standing up the operating model for enterprise AI—platforms, people, and governance designed for durable business outcomes.

items.title: Spark-era data & context-aware AI
items.challenge: Next-generation telecom and enterprise products needed a coherent Big Data and AI strategy across U.S. and China teams.
items.action: Led global technology strategy for Big Data and AI product innovation; defined Spark-based infrastructure vision and context-aware AI system architecture.
items.impact: Shaped product direction for modern data infrastructure and intelligent systems ahead of the mainstream enterprise wave.

items.title: Three U.S. patents in mobile intelligence
items.challenge: Mobile systems needed better compression, security trust models, and behavior-aware companions—problems that required invention, not incremental features.
items.action: Invented across text-based message compression, trust-blueprint security architectures, and user behavior modeling for intelligent mobile companions.
items.impact: 3 U.S. patents; a track record of turning systems insight into durable IP.

items.title: Human-powered AI for special-needs families
items.challenge: Caregivers of neurodiverse children faced fragmented, untrusted information about meltdowns, therapy access, and public support.
items.action: Co-founded and built an LLM-powered care platform as CPTO—agentic advice grounded in trusted experience, community, and access pathways.
items.impact: Shipped a working product prototype; learned hard GTM truths and carried a founder’s builder mindset back into executive AI leadership.
